result: A high-quality chromosome-level genome assembly of M. dirhodum was generated using PacBio HiFi reads and Hi-C technology. The final assembly is 447.8 Mb with 98.50% anchored to nine chromosomes, contig N50 of 7.82 Mb, scaffold N50 of 37.54 Mb, and 18,003 protein-coding genes with 92.05% functionally annotated. BUSCO analysis showed 96.9% completeness, higher than several other aphid species.
evaluation: Claims C27-C55, C131-C133 collectively provide comprehensive evidence for a high-quality genome assembly. The sequencing coverage (92.22×), assembly metrics (N50 values, chromosome anchoring), quality assessment (BUSCO scores), and annotation statistics are all well-documented with specific values. The comparisons to other aphid genomes provide context for quality assessment.

result: Phylogenetic and synteny analyses revealed that M. dirhodum is closely related to A. pisum within the Aphididae cluster. Synteny analysis showed high levels of genome rearrangement between M. dirhodum and A. pisum, with Chr1 in M. dirhodum sharing 81.9% syntenic blocks with chr X in A. pisum, suggesting Chr1 is the sex chromosome.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by orthology analysis (209,881 genes in 22,945 orthogroups) and synteny comparisons shown in Figure 1C-D. The phylogenetic placement and chromosomal relationships are clearly demonstrated with specific percentages and visual evidence.

result: A total of 11,678 A-to-I RNA-editing sites were systematically identified in M. dirhodum, representing the first systematic identification of RNA-editing events in aphids. These sites are distributed across all nine chromosomes with 62.7% in protein-coding genes, including 515 nonsynonymous and 1485 synonymous sites.
evaluation: Claims C28, C60-C63, C108-C109 are supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 2. The distribution, density, and classification of editing sites are quantified with specific numbers and percentages. The novelty claim (first in aphids) is explicitly stated.

result: Two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites on CYP18A1 (sites 528 and 759) are closely associated with crowding-induced transgenerational wing dimorphism. Crowding increased winged offspring by 36.4%, which was reversed by 20E treatment (31.2% decrease). The editing proportions at these sites were significantly higher under crowding (93.3% and 36.4%) compared to normal conditions (21.3% and 20.0%), correlating with increased CYP18A1 expression and decreased 20E titer.
evaluation: Claims C29, C65-C73 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3. The wing dimorphism phenotype, editing site proportions, gene expression changes (RT-qPCR and Western blot), and 20E titer measurements are all quantified with statistical significance. Sample sizes are provided (n=255-277 offspring). The causal inference (C73) is appropriately stated as an inference.

result: ADAR2 regulates the A-to-I RNA-editing level of CYP18A1 to control maternal 20E titer and wing dimorphism. RNAi knockdown of ADAR2 reduced CYP18A1 expression by 42.2%, decreased editing at sites 528 and 759 by 61.3% and 22.4%, increased 20E titer, and reduced winged offspring by 24.4%. ADAR2 expression was induced by 20E (2.19-fold) but not by crowding alone.
evaluation: Claims C74-C84 are supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4. The knockdown efficiency, effects on editing levels, CYP18A1 expression, 20E titer, and wing phenotype are all quantified with appropriate controls (dsEGFP). Sample sizes are provided (n=248-273 offspring). The mechanistic conclusion (C84) is appropriately stated as an inference from the experimental results.

result: miR-3036-5p targets CYP18A1 at a site containing editing position 528, and A-to-I RNA editing at this site reduces miR-3036-5p binding. miR-3036-5p expression decreased by 48.8% after crowding. RIP assays, FISH colocalization, and luciferase reporter assays demonstrated that miR-3036-5p binds to unedited CYP18A1 (52.7% reduction in luciferase activity) but binding is reduced when the site is edited (39.2% difference between edited and unedited).
evaluation: Claims C86-C94 are supported by multiple complementary experiments shown in Figure 5: bioinformatic prediction, expression analysis, RIP assays, FISH colocalization, and luciferase reporter assays. The luciferase experiments include appropriate controls (mutated binding site, empty vector) and demonstrate the effect of editing on miR-3036-5p binding with statistical significance.

result: Under normal conditions, miR-3036-5p inhibition increased CYP18A1 expression (2.89-fold), decreased 20E titer (31.0%), and increased winged offspring (19.2%), while miR-3036-5p overexpression had no effect on wing phenotype. Under crowding conditions, neither miR-3036-5p inhibition nor overexpression affected CYP18A1 expression or wing dimorphism, likely because high A-to-I RNA editing levels destroy the miR-3036-5p binding site.
evaluation: Claims C95-C100, C123-C125, C134-C135 are supported by miRNA manipulation experiments shown in Figure 6. The differential effects under normal versus crowding conditions are clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls and sample sizes (n=249-267 offspring). The mechanistic interpretation linking editing levels to miR-3036-5p function is logically consistent with the luciferase data from the previous result.

result: This work demonstrates that A-to-I RNA editing is a dynamic mechanism regulating transgenerational wing dimorphism in aphids and represents the first report of A-to-I RNA editing involvement in insect developmental polyphenism. The findings suggest insects use RNA editing as a mechanism to adapt to environmental pressure and generate phenotypic plasticity.
evaluation: Claims C32, C129-C130 represent the major conclusions drawn from the collective experimental evidence. The novelty claim (first report in insect polyphenism) is explicitly stated. The broader inference about RNA editing as an adaptive mechanism (C129) is appropriately supported by the experimental data showing environment-responsive editing changes that affect phenotype.

result: M. dirhodum is an economically important aphid pest of cereals worldwide, native to the Holarctic and introduced to multiple continents. It damages crops through direct feeding, honeydew production, and virus transmission, causing yield losses of 27-30% during wheat flowering stages.
evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide background information about M. dirhodum and are supported by multiple literature citations. These establish the agricultural importance and justify the study organism selection.

result: Wing polymorphism is common in insects and M. dirhodum can produce wing morphs in response to environmental cues. Aphids differ from planthoppers in that wing polymorphism is transgenerational rather than within-generation. 20E is an essential regulatory factor in aphid wing dimorphism, with elevated maternal ecdysone signaling suppressing embryonic IIS signaling to produce wingless offspring.
evaluation: Claims C9-C22 provide background on wing polymorphism and 20E signaling, supported by literature citations. These establish the biological context and prior knowledge that motivates the current study's focus on 20E pathway genes.

result: A-to-I RNA editing is the most prevalent RNA post-transcriptional modification, catalyzed by ADAR enzymes. It acts through multiple mechanisms and plays important roles in development, reproduction, and environmental responses. However, research on A-to-I RNA editing in insects, especially agricultural pests, is limited.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26, C105-C107 provide background on RNA editing, supported by literature citations. These establish the biological significance of RNA editing and identify the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

result: CYP18A1 is a key enzyme in 20E metabolism that can cause developmental disorders when abnormally expressed. High population density induces winged morphs in aphids, and CYP18A1 is involved in crowding-mediated wing dimorphism. A-to-I RNA-editing levels are affected by environmental changes, as demonstrated in other organisms.
evaluation: Claims C30, C64, C110-C118 provide background on CYP18A1 function and environmental effects on RNA editing, supported by literature citations. These establish the rationale for investigating CYP18A1 editing in the context of crowding-induced wing dimorphism.

result: RNA editing of miRNA binding sites can alter miRNA targeting, creating or destroying binding sites. This has been demonstrated in various organisms including yak and human cells, where editing affects gene expression and cellular phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C85, C119-C121 provide background on RNA editing effects on miRNA binding, supported by literature citations. These establish precedent for the mechanism investigated in the current study.

result: Aphids are important agricultural pests and models for studying symbiosis, insect-plant interactions, and developmental polyphenism. Over 20 aphid genomes have been assembled, and this study produced the first high-quality chromosome-level genome of M. dirhodum using PacBio HiFi reads and Hi-C technology.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 provide context for the genomic work and state the novelty of the genome assembly. These are supported by literature citations and the experimental data presented.

result: Epigenetic modifications including RNA editing are proposed mechanisms for regulating phenotypic plasticity. RNA editing is hypothesized as an adaptive strategy in cephalopods, where squid employ temperature-responsive RNA editing that enhances protein function in cold conditions.
evaluation: Claims C122, C126-C128 provide comparative context from cephalopod studies, supported by literature citations. These establish precedent for RNA editing as an adaptive mechanism for phenotypic plasticity, supporting the broader significance of the aphid findings.
